lesson.title: Inverse trigonometric functions: domain, range, principal values and graphs

coverage.section: Definition of the inverse trigonometric functions
Domain, range and principal value branches
Domain, range and principal value branches
Domain, range and principal value branches

blocks.text: Why trigonometric functions need restricting

The function $y=\sin x$ takes the value $\tfrac12$ at $x=\tfrac{\pi}{6},\ \tfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \tfrac{13\pi}{6},\dots$ and at infinitely many other points. A function has an inverse only if it is **one-one (injective)** and **onto its codomain**. Over the whole real line, none of the six trigonometric functions is one-one, so none has an inverse.

To obtain an inverse we cut out a part of the domain on which the function is one-one and still takes **all** its values. Such a piece is called a **branch**. The branch that contains the angle $0$ (or is nearest to it) and is used by convention is the **principal value branch**.

For example, $\sin x$ is increasing and takes every value from $-1$ to $1$ exactly once on $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$. So the restricted function $\sin:\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\to[-1,1]$ is a bijection and has an inverse.
Definition of the inverse trigonometric functions
$\sin^{-1}x=y$ means $\sin y=x$ with $y\in\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ and $x\in[-1,1]$. The symbol $\sin^{-1}x$ is read "arc sine of $x$" and is **not** $\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$.

$\cos^{-1}x=y$ means $\cos y=x$ with $y\in[0,\pi]$. $\tan^{-1}x=y$ means $\tan y=x$ with $y\in\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. The other three ($\cot^{-1},\sec^{-1},\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}$) are defined the same way on their own branches.

In words: an inverse trigonometric function takes a **ratio** and returns the **unique angle in the principal branch** with that ratio. Whenever you are asked for a "principal value", the answer must lie in the range given in the table below, whatever the question looks like.
Domain, range and principal value branches

blocks.caption: Domain and range (principal value branch) of the six inverse functions

blocks.text: The domain of an inverse function equals the range of the original function, and the range of the inverse equals the restricted domain of the original. So $\sin^{-1}$ accepts only numbers from $-1$ to $1$, because $\sin$ produces only those. A number such as $\sin^{-1}2$ does not exist.

Memory aid: the "sin, tan, cosec" family has branches centred on $0$ (between $-\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$). The "cos, cot, sec" family has branches that start at $0$ and end at $\pi$. So $\cos^{-1}$ never returns a negative angle.

blocks.problem: Find the principal value of (i) $\sin^{-1}\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$ and (ii) $\cos^{-1}\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\right)$.
blocks.solution:
(i) Let $y=\sin^{-1}\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$, so $\sin y=-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ with $y\in\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$. We know $\sin\tfrac{\pi}{3}=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and sine is odd, so $y=-\tfrac{\pi}{3}$, which lies in the branch.

(ii) Let $y=\cos^{-1}\left(-\tfrac12\right)$, so $\cos y=-\tfrac12$ with $y\in[0,\pi]$. The reference angle is $\tfrac{\pi}{3}$ and cosine is negative in the second quadrant, so $y=\pi-\tfrac{\pi}{3}=\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

blocks.text: Properties and simple identities
Negative arguments: $\sin^{-1}$ and $\tan^{-1}$ are odd functions. For $\cos^{-1}$ subtract from $\pi$, so the result stays in $[0,\pi]$. Valid for $x\in[-1,1]$ ($\tan^{-1}$: all real $x$).
Complementary pairs. The first holds for $x\in[-1,1]$, the second for every real $x$. Likewise $\sec^{-1}x+\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ for $|x|\ge1$.

A function followed by its inverse returns the input only when the input lies in the correct set. If $\theta$ is outside the branch, first move it into the branch using the periodicity and sign rules of the trigonometric function.
Addition formula. If $xy>1$ and $x,y>0$, add $\pi$ to the right-hand side. If $xy>1$ and $x,y<0$, subtract $\pi$.
Double-angle forms, each valid only in the stated range of $x$.

blocks.solution: The angle $\tfrac{3\pi}{4}$ is not in $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, so the answer is not $\tfrac{3\pi}{4}$. First compute $\sin\tfrac{3\pi}{4}=\sin\left(\pi-\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\sin\tfrac{\pi}{4}=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$. Now $\sin^{-1}\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ is the angle in $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ whose sine is $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$, namely $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Here $xy=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac13=\tfrac16<1$, so the plain formula applies: $\tan^{-1}\tfrac12+\tan^{-1}\tfrac13=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\tfrac12+\tfrac13}{1-\tfrac16}=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{5/6}{5/6}=\tan^{-1}1=\tfrac{\pi}{4}$.

blocks.text: Common mistake: writing $\sin^{-1}(\sin x)=x$ for every $x$. It is true only for $x\in\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$. For example $\cos^{-1}(\cos 2\pi)=0$, not $2\pi$, and $\sin^{-1}(\sin\pi)=0$, not $\pi$.
Graphs of inverse trigonometric functions
The graph of an inverse function is the **mirror image of the graph of the restricted original function in the line $y=x$**. Points $(a,b)$ on $y=\sin x$ become $(b,a)$ on $y=\sin^{-1}x$.

blocks.caption: Shape of each graph
rows: Increasing curve through $(-1,-\tfrac{\pi}{2}),(0,0),(1,\tfrac{\pi}{2})$, passing through the origin and defined only for $-1\le x\le1$. It is odd (symmetric about the origin).
Decreasing curve from $(-1,\pi)$ through $(0,\tfrac{\pi}{2})$ to $(1,0)$. It is neither odd nor even.
Increasing, odd, passes through the origin; has horizontal asymptotes $y=\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $y=-\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ and is defined for all real $x$.
Decreasing, between the asymptotes $y=\pi$ (left) and $y=0$ (right); crosses the $y$-axis at $(0,\tfrac{\pi}{2})$.
Two pieces: one for $x\le-1$ with $y$ from $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ (asymptote) to $\pi$, and one for $x\ge1$ with $y$ from $0$ to $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ (asymptote). Nothing exists for $-1<x<1$.
Two pieces: for $x\le-1$, $y$ from $-\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ to $0$ (asymptote); for $x\ge1$, $y$ from $0$ (asymptote) to $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. Nothing exists for $-1<x<1$.

blocks.text: Reading values from the graph is a quick check. On $y=\cos^{-1}x$, the point $(0,\tfrac{\pi}{2})$ shows $\cos^{-1}0=\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. On $y=\tan^{-1}x$, large positive $x$ gives values approaching but never reaching $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $\tan^{-1}x<\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ for every real $x$.

Principal ranges to remember: $\sin^{-1}$: $[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}]$; $\cos^{-1}$: $[0,\pi]$; $\tan^{-1}$: $(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2})$; $\cot^{-1}$: $(0,\pi)$. Square brackets mean the end values are attained; round brackets mean they are not.
Always reduce first: to evaluate $f^{-1}(f(\theta))$, bring $\theta$ into the principal branch of $f^{-1}$, then read the value. Check that your final answer lies inside the range in the table.

Exam tip: for $\sin^{-1}x$ and $\cos^{-1}x$ the argument must satisfy $|x|\le1$; for $\sec^{-1}$ and $\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}$ it must satisfy $|x|\ge1$. Many "find the domain" questions are just this check applied to a linear expression, such as $-1\le 2x-1\le 1$.

questions.stem: What is the principal value of $\sin^{-1}\left(\tfrac12\right)$?
questions.explanation: We need the angle $y$ in $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ with $\sin y=\tfrac12$. Since $\sin\tfrac{\pi}{6}=\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$ lies in the principal branch, $\sin^{-1}\tfrac12=\tfrac{\pi}{6}$. The other solution $\tfrac{5\pi}{6}$ is outside the branch and is rejected.
questions.objective: Find the principal value of sin inverse for a standard ratio

questions.stem: The range of the principal value branch of $\cos^{-1}x$ is
questions.explanation: Cosine is decreasing and one-one on $[0,\pi]$, taking every value from $1$ down to $-1$. Hence the principal branch of $\cos^{-1}$ is $[0,\pi]$, with $\cos^{-1}1=0$ and $\cos^{-1}(-1)=\pi$ both attained, so the interval is closed at both ends.

optionRationale.1: This is the range of sin inverse, not cos inverse.
optionRationale.3: The end points are attained: cos inverse of 1 is 0 and of -1 is pi, so the interval is closed. Open interval is for cot inverse.
optionRationale.4: Cos inverse never returns a negative angle.

questions.objective: State the range of cos inverse

questions.stem: The domain of $\sin^{-1}x$ is
questions.explanation: The domain of an inverse function is the range of the original function. Over the restricted branch, $\sin$ takes every value from $-1$ to $1$ and no others, so $\sin^{-1}x$ is defined exactly for $-1\le x\le1$, end points included.

optionRationale.1: Sine never exceeds 1 in magnitude, so sin inverse is not defined for all reals; R is the domain of tan inverse.
optionRationale.2: This is the range of sin inverse, not its domain.
optionRationale.4: The end values are included: sin inverse of 1 is pi/2 and of -1 is -pi/2.

questions.objective: State the domain of sin inverse

questions.stem: Negative argument for cos inverse: The principal value of $\cos^{-1}\left(-\tfrac12\right)$ is
questions.explanation: Using $\cos^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\cos^{-1}x$, we get $\cos^{-1}\left(-\tfrac12\right)=\pi-\tfrac{\pi}{3}=\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$. This lies in $[0,\pi]$ and $\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{3}=-\tfrac12$, confirming the answer.

optionRationale.1: Negative angles are outside the principal branch [0, pi] of cos inverse.
optionRationale.2: This is $\cos^{-1}\tfrac12$; the sign of the argument was ignored.

questions.objective: Use the negative-argument rule for cos inverse

questions.stem: Odd-function property: The principal value of $\tan^{-1}\left(-\sqrt3\right)$ is
questions.explanation: Since $\tan^{-1}$ is an odd function, $\tan^{-1}(-\sqrt3)=-\tan^{-1}\sqrt3=-\tfrac{\pi}{3}$. Check: $\tan\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=-\sqrt3$ and $-\tfrac{\pi}{3}\in\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

optionRationale.2: This is tan inverse of positive root 3; tan inverse is odd, so the sign changes.
optionRationale.3: tan(2pi/3) = -root 3 but 2pi/3 is outside the branch (-pi/2, pi/2).

questions.objective: Use oddness of tan inverse

questions.stem: Angle outside the branch: The value of $\sin^{-1}\left(\sin\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ is
questions.explanation: First $\sin\tfrac{2\pi}{3}=\sin\left(\pi-\tfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. Then $\sin^{-1}\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is the angle in $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ with that sine, which is $\tfrac{\pi}{3}$. The angle $\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$ had to be brought into the branch.

optionRationale.1: This ignores the principal branch; 2pi/3 is not in [-pi/2, pi/2].

questions.objective: Evaluate sin inverse of sin for an angle outside the branch

questions.stem: Complementary identity: The value of $\sin^{-1}\tfrac35+\cos^{-1}\tfrac35$ is
questions.explanation: For every $x\in[-1,1]$, $\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. The argument $\tfrac35$ lies in $[-1,1]$, so the sum is $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ without computing either angle. (Check: $\sin^{-1}0.6\approx 36.87^\circ$ and $\cos^{-1}0.6\approx53.13^\circ$, which add to $90^\circ$.)

optionRationale.1: The sum of the two inverses is pi/2, not pi.
optionRationale.2: The angles are not added as ratios; the identity gives a constant angle.
optionRationale.4: pi/4 would need the two angles to be equal, which they are not here.

questions.objective: Apply the complementary identity

questions.stem: Secant branch: The principal value of $\sec^{-1}(2)$ is
questions.explanation: $\sec^{-1}2=y$ means $\sec y=2$, i.e. $\cos y=\tfrac12$ with $y\in[0,\pi]$, $y\neq\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. Hence $y=\tfrac{\pi}{3}$. The argument $2$ satisfies $|x|\ge1$, so it is in the domain.
questions.objective: Evaluate sec inverse using the reciprocal of cos

questions.stem: Cosecant branch with a negative argument: The principal value of $\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-2)$ is
questions.explanation: $\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-2)=y$ means $\sin y=-\tfrac12$ with $y\in\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, $y\neq0$. So $y=-\tfrac{\pi}{6}$. Equivalently $\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-x)=-\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x$, giving $-\tfrac{\pi}{6}$.

optionRationale.2: The sign is lost: cosec inverse is odd, so a negative argument gives a negative angle.
optionRationale.4: The cosec inverse branch is [-pi/2, pi/2] minus {0}; 7pi/6 lies outside it.

questions.objective: Evaluate cosec inverse of a negative argument

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about principal value branches.
A. The range of $\tan^{-1}x$ is $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.
B. The range of $\cot^{-1}x$ is $(0,\pi)$.
C. The range of $\cos^{-1}x$ is $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$.
D. The domain of $\sec^{-1}x$ is $\mathbb{R}-(-1,1)$.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A is correct: tan inverse never reaches $\pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. B is correct: cot inverse lies strictly between $0$ and $\pi$. C is wrong: the range of cos inverse is $[0,\pi]$, and $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ belongs to sin inverse. D is correct: secant takes values with $|y|\ge1$ only. So A, B and D are correct.

optionRationale.2: Statement C is false, so C cannot be included.
optionRationale.3: It leaves out A, which is correct, and includes the false statement C.
optionRationale.4: It omits B, which is correct.

questions.objective: Recall domains and ranges of the inverse functions

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The function $\sin x$ has an inverse only after its domain is restricted, for example to $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$.
Reason (R): $\sin x$ is not one-one on $\mathbb{R}$, because different angles can have the same sine.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Both statements are true. On $\mathbb{R}$, $\sin 0=\sin\pi=0$, so sine is many-one and cannot have an inverse. Restricting to $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ makes it one-one and onto $[-1,1]$. The failure of one-one-ness is exactly why the restriction is needed, so R explains A.

optionRationale.2: R is not merely true; it is the direct reason the restriction is required.
optionRationale.3: R is true: sin 0 = sin pi although 0 and pi differ.
optionRationale.4: A is true: the principal branch is exactly a restriction of the domain.

questions.objective: Explain why principal branches are needed

questions.stem: Match the inverse functions in List-I with their principal value ranges in List-II.
questions.explanation: $\sin^{-1}$ has range $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ (III). $\cos^{-1}$ has range $[0,\pi]$ (I). $\tan^{-1}$ has the open range $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ (IV). $\cot^{-1}$ has the open range $(0,\pi)$ (II). So the matching is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

optionRationale.2: It swaps sin inverse and cos inverse ranges.
optionRationale.3: It swaps the open ranges of tan inverse and cot inverse.
optionRationale.4: It assigns the closed range of sin inverse to tan inverse and the open one to sin inverse.

questions.objective: Match each inverse function with its range

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): $\sin^{-1}\left(\sin\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)=\tfrac{3\pi}{4}$.
Reason (R): The principal value branch of $\sin^{-1}$ is $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: $\sin\tfrac{3\pi}{4}=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ and $\sin^{-1}\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}=\tfrac{\pi}{4}$, because $\tfrac{3\pi}{4}$ is outside the branch. The reason is a true statement and is in fact why the assertion fails. So A is false but R is true.

optionRationale.1: A is false, so R cannot explain it as a true statement.
optionRationale.2: A is false: the correct value is pi/4.
optionRationale.3: R is true, the principal branch of sin inverse is indeed [-pi/2, pi/2].

questions.objective: Recognise that sin inverse of sin returns the angle only inside the branch

questions.stem: Angle beyond pi: The value of $\cos^{-1}\left(\cos\tfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)$ is
questions.explanation: $\cos\tfrac{7\pi}{6}=\cos\left(\pi+\tfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\cos\tfrac{\pi}{6}=-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. Then $\cos^{-1}\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=\pi-\tfrac{\pi}{6}=\tfrac{5\pi}{6}$, which lies in $[0,\pi]$. Equivalently $\cos\tfrac{7\pi}{6}=\cos\left(2\pi-\tfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)=\cos\tfrac{5\pi}{6}$.

optionRationale.1: This lies outside [0, pi]; the angle has to be brought into the branch.
optionRationale.3: Cos inverse never gives a negative value.

questions.objective: Evaluate cos inverse of cos for an angle beyond pi

questions.stem: Sum of three arctangents: The value of $\tan^{-1}1+\tan^{-1}2+\tan^{-1}3$ is
questions.explanation: $\tan^{-1}1=\tfrac{\pi}{4}$. For $2$ and $3$, $xy=6>1$ with both positive, so $\tan^{-1}2+\tan^{-1}3=\pi+\tan^{-1}\dfrac{5}{1-6}=\pi+\tan^{-1}(-1)=\pi-\tfrac{\pi}{4}=\tfrac{3\pi}{4}$. The total is $\tfrac{\pi}{4}+\tfrac{3\pi}{4}=\pi$. Numerically $45^\circ+63.43^\circ+71.57^\circ=180^\circ$.

optionRationale.1: Using the formula without checking $xy<1$ for $2$ and $3$ (here $xy=6>1$) gives this wrong value.
optionRationale.2: This is only $\tan^{-1}2+\tan^{-1}3$; the $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$ from $\tan^{-1}1$ has been left out.
optionRationale.4: This adds the extra pi twice.

questions.objective: Add inverse tangents when xy exceeds 1

questions.stem: Compound-angle problem: The value of $\sin\left(\tan^{-1}\tfrac34+\cos^{-1}\tfrac{5}{13}\right)$ is
questions.explanation: Let $A=\tan^{-1}\tfrac34$: then $\sin A=\tfrac35,\ \cos A=\tfrac45$. Let $B=\cos^{-1}\tfrac5{13}$: then $\cos B=\tfrac5{13},\ \sin B=\tfrac{12}{13}$. So $\sin(A+B)=\sin A\cos B+\cos A\sin B=\tfrac35\cdot\tfrac5{13}+\tfrac45\cdot\tfrac{12}{13}=\tfrac{15+48}{65}=\tfrac{63}{65}$.

optionRationale.1: This is $\sin(A-B)=\tfrac{15-48}{65}$, the sine of the difference, not the sum.
optionRationale.2: This is $\cos(A-B)=\tfrac{20+36}{65}$, a cosine formula, not the required sine of the sum.
optionRationale.3: This is $\cos(A+B)=\tfrac{20-36}{65}$, the cosine of the sum, not its sine.

questions.objective: Combine inverse functions using compound-angle formulas

questions.stem: Double-angle form: $2\tan^{-1}\left(\tfrac12\right)$ is equal to
questions.explanation: With $x=\tfrac12$ (so $|x|<1$): $2\tan^{-1}x=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1-x^2}=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{1-\tfrac14}=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{3/4}=\tan^{-1}\tfrac43$. As a check $2\times26.565^\circ=53.13^\circ=\tan^{-1}\tfrac43$.

optionRationale.2: This is the value of tan(2A) inverted: with x = 1/2, 2x/(1 - x^2) = 4/3, not 3/4.

questions.objective: Use the double-angle form of tan inverse

questions.stem: Large angle in radians: The value of $\cos^{-1}(\cos 10)$, where $10$ is in radians, is
questions.explanation: We need an angle in $[0,\pi]$ with the same cosine as $10$. Since cosine has period $2\pi$ and is even, $\cos10=\cos(4\pi-10)$. Numerically $4\pi\approx12.566$, so $4\pi-10\approx2.566$, which lies in $[0,\pi]\approx[0,3.1416]$. Hence $\cos^{-1}(\cos10)=4\pi-10$.

optionRationale.1: Ten radians is far outside [0, pi], so the answer cannot be 10.
optionRationale.3: $\cos(10-3\pi)=-\cos10$, so this has the opposite cosine.
optionRationale.4: $3\pi-10\approx-0.575$ is negative and so outside the range of $\cos^{-1}$.

questions.objective: Reduce a large angle into the principal branch of cos inverse

questions.stem: The solution of $\tan^{-1}(x+1)+\tan^{-1}(x-1)=\tan^{-1}\tfrac{8}{31}$ is
questions.explanation: Using the addition formula, $\dfrac{(x+1)+(x-1)}{1-(x^2-1)}=\dfrac{2x}{2-x^2}=\dfrac{8}{31}$, so $62x=16-8x^2$, i.e. $4x^2+31x-8=0$, giving $x=\dfrac{-31\pm33}{8}$, that is $x=\tfrac14$ or $x=-8$. The formula needs $(x+1)(x-1)<1$. For $x=\tfrac14$ the product is $-\tfrac{15}{16}<1$, valid. For $x=-8$ it is $63>1$, so it is rejected. Hence $x=\tfrac14$.

optionRationale.1: Substituting $x=-8$ gives two large negative angles ($\tan^{-1}(-7)+\tan^{-1}(-9)$), whose sum is negative, not $\tan^{-1}\tfrac{8}{31}>0$. It satisfies the algebra but not the equation.
optionRationale.2: x = -8 is extraneous because (x+1)(x-1) = 63 > 1, so the simple addition formula was not valid for it.
optionRationale.4: For $x=4$ the left side is $\tan^{-1}5+\tan^{-1}3\approx 78.7^\circ+71.6^\circ=150.3^\circ$, not $\tan^{-1}\tfrac8{31}\approx14.4^\circ$.

questions.objective: Solve an inverse trigonometric equation and test validity of the addition formula

questions.stem: The domain of the function $f(x)=\sin^{-1}(2x-1)$ is
questions.explanation: $\sin^{-1}$ needs its argument in $[-1,1]$, so $-1\le2x-1\le1$. Adding $1$: $0\le2x\le2$. Dividing by $2$: $0\le x\le1$. Hence the domain is $[0,1]$, and the end points are included because $\sin^{-1}(\pm1)$ exist.

optionRationale.1: This is the domain of sin inverse itself, but here the argument is 2x - 1, which must lie in [-1, 1].
optionRationale.3: The upper limit is wrong: 2x - 1 <= 1 gives x <= 1.

questions.objective: Find the domain of a composite inverse trigonometric function
